opening_message:
Ticket 1: Timothy Wallace (employee ID E022) requests admin access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E022.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Engineer (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Timothy Wallace (E022) is a full-time Engineer requesting admin on Payroll. Payroll is owned by the Payroll Specialist role, so as an Engineer admin is not permitted; maximum for full-time employees is write. Recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Engineer (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1 by HR agent)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Timothy Wallace (E022) is a contractor with basic security training (note in memory says full-time, but DB is authoritative). Contractors with basic training are limited to read; they never get admin. Requested admin exceeds maximum, so recommend read.
reason: Timothy Wallace (E022) requested admin on Payroll. HR (authoritative for employment type) confirms he is a full-time Engineer. Payroll is owned by the Payroll Specialist role, not Engineer, so admin is not permitted for him; the maximum for full-time employees is write. Since requested admin exceeds the maximum, grant write.

- Security agent says: role Engineer (not looked up), employment type contractor (looked up in own DB), security training basic, recommendation read. Comment: Security DB shows contractor with basic security training, limited to read; never admin. Requested admin exceeds max, so recommend read.

So there's a conflict: HR says full-time, Security says contractor. The security agent noted that memory says full-time, but DB is authoritative. Hmm.

Which to trust? The policy: full_time employees up to write; admin only if role owns system. Engineer doesn't own Payroll, so full-time max is write. Contractor: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

Requested: admin. Both cases, admin is above maximum. So maximum is write (if full-time) or read (if contractor with basic training).

The conflicting facts matter: if full-time, grant write; if contractor basic, grant read.

Which facts are authoritative? The Security agent looked up employment type in own database and says contractor; HR looked up in own database and says full-time. Both claim lookup. The security note says DB is authoritative. But we have two databases claiming different things. As Approver, we need to decide.

Security agent note: contractor with basic security training. Max read. Recommend read.

The requested level is admin. Under either interpretation, admin exceeds maximum, so grant max. The maximum differs: write vs read.

I think the most defensible decision: Grant the maximum allowed. Given uncertainty, hmm.

Actually, let's re-read the policy: maximum access levels. For full_time: up to write. Admin only if role owns system. Engineer doesn't own Payroll. So max = write. For contractor: read, or write if advanced security training. Basic training -> read. Never admin.
